questions.q: The colligative property used for the determination of molar mass of polymers and proteins is :
questions.solution:
Polymers and proteins have very **large** molar masses, so even a gram of them dissolved in a litre gives a tiny molality. All four colligative properties are proportional to molality, so all four give a small effect — the question is which one is still **measurable**.

For a $0 \cdot 001$ m solution :

- depression in freezing point is about $0 \cdot 002$ K,
- elevation in boiling point is about $0 \cdot 0005$ K,

both far too small to measure reliably with an ordinary thermometer.

**Osmotic pressure**, however, is $\pi = CRT$, and at 300 K a $0 \cdot 001$ M solution gives

$$\pi = 0 \cdot 001 \times 0 \cdot 0821 \times 300 \approx 0 \cdot 025\ \text{atm} \approx 19\ \text{mm Hg},$$

which is easily measured. Two further advantages: it is measured **at room temperature**, so a protein is not denatured by heating, and it uses molarity rather than molality.

That is why osmotic pressure is the method of choice for macromolecules.

questions.q: For an ideal solution of two volatile liquids, the total vapour pressure is:
questions.solution:
Raoult's law: each component contributes in proportion to its **own** mole fraction in the liquid.

$p_{\text{total}} = \mathbf{p_{A}^{0}x_{A} + p_{B}^{0}x_{B}}$.

A room half full of people from each of two towns: each town contributes its share of the noise.

questions.q: Which of these is **not** a colligative property?
questions.solution:
Colligative properties depend only on the **number** of solute particles, not on what they are: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, osmotic pressure.

**Optical rotation** depends entirely on the identity and structure of the molecule, so it is not colligative.

questions.q: The van't Hoff factor for $\text{NaCl}$ in dilute aqueous solution, assuming complete dissociation, is:
questions.solution:
$\text{NaCl} \to \text{Na}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}$ — one formula unit gives **two** particles, so $i = \mathbf{2}$.

For $\text{CaCl}_{2}$ it would be 3. Association, as with acetic acid in benzene, makes $i$ **less** than 1.

questions.q: According to Henry's law, the solubility of a gas in a liquid:
questions.solution:
$p = K_{H}x$ — the partial pressure of the gas is proportional to its mole fraction in solution.

It is why a fizzy drink releases gas the moment the cap is opened, and why divers get the bends coming up too fast.

Solubility of a gas **decreases** with temperature, which is why warm soda goes flat quickly.
options: is proportional to its partial pressure
is proportional to the square of pressure

questions.q: Find the molarity of a solution containing $4$ g of $\text{NaOH}$ in $500$ mL of solution. (Molar mass of $\text{NaOH} = 40$ g/mol.)
questions.solution:
Moles $= \dfrac{4}{40} = 0.1$ mol.

Molarity $= \dfrac{0.1\text{ mol}}{0.5\text{ L}} = \mathbf{0.2}$ M.

questions.q: A solution contains $2$ mol of solute and $8$ mol of solvent. Find the mole fraction of the solute.
questions.solution:
$x_{\text{solute}} = \dfrac{2}{2 + 8} = \mathbf{0.2}$.

The two mole fractions always add to 1, so the solvent's is $0.8$.

questions.q: Find the elevation in boiling point (in K) when $0.5$ mol of a non-electrolyte is dissolved in $1$ kg of water. ($K_{b} = 0.52$ K kg/mol.)
questions.solution:
$\Delta T_{b} = K_{b}\,m = 0.52 \times 0.5 = \mathbf{0.26}$ K.

The solute particles occupy part of the surface, so fewer solvent molecules escape and a higher temperature is needed to reach atmospheric pressure.

questions.q: Find the freezing point (in °C) of a solution of molality $0.2$ m in water. ($K_{f} = 1.86$ K kg/mol.)
questions.solution:
$\Delta T_{f} = K_{f}\,m = 1.86 \times 0.2 = 0.372$ K.

The solution freezes **below** $0$ °C: $\mathbf{-0.372}$ °C.

It is why salt is spread on icy roads, and why antifreeze works.

questions.q: Find the osmotic pressure (in atm) of a $0.1$ M solution at $300$ K. Take $R = 0.0821$ L atm K$^{-1}$mol$^{-1}$, correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
$\pi = CRT = 0.1 \times 0.0821 \times 300 = \mathbf{2.46}$ atm.

Osmotic pressure is the largest of the colligative effects by far, which is why it is the one used to find the molar mass of proteins — a measurable pressure from a tiny concentration.

questions.q: State Raoult's law for a solution of two volatile liquids and explain positive and negative deviations with one example each.
questions.solution:
**Raoult's law.** For each component, the partial vapour pressure is its pure vapour pressure times its mole fraction in the liquid:

$p_{A} = p_{A}^{0}x_{A}$, $\quad p_{B} = p_{B}^{0}x_{B}$, $\quad p_{\text{total}} = p_{A} + p_{B}$.

An **ideal solution** obeys this at every composition, with $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} = 0$ and $\Delta V_{\text{mix}} = 0$ — the A–B forces are the same strength as A–A and B–B.

**Positive deviation.** A–B attraction is **weaker** than A–A and B–B, so molecules escape more readily than expected: vapour pressure higher than Raoult predicts, $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0$ (endothermic), volume increases.

**Example: ethanol + water.** Ethanol's hydrogen bonds to water are weaker than water's to itself. These mixtures form a **minimum-boiling azeotrope**.

**Negative deviation.** A–B attraction is **stronger**, so molecules are held back: vapour pressure lower than predicted, $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} < 0$ (exothermic), volume decreases.

**Example: chloroform + acetone**, which hydrogen-bond to each other. These form a **maximum-boiling azeotrope**.

An azeotrope boils without changing composition, which is exactly why fractional distillation cannot produce absolute alcohol from a water mixture.

questions.q: Explain how the depression of freezing point is used to determine the molar mass of a solute, and derive the working formula.
questions.solution:
$\Delta T_{f} = K_{f}\,m$, and molality is

$m = \dfrac{w_{2}/M_{2}}{w_{1}\text{ (in kg)}}$

where $w_{2}$ is the solute mass, $M_{2}$ its molar mass, $w_{1}$ the solvent mass.

Substituting and rearranging:

$\mathbf{M_{2} = \dfrac{K_{f} \times w_{2} \times 1000}{\Delta T_{f} \times w_{1}\text{(g)}}}$.

**In practice:** measure the pure solvent's freezing point, dissolve a weighed sample, measure again, and put the numbers in.

**The catch.** The method counts **particles**, so for anything that dissociates (a salt) or associates (a carboxylic acid in benzene) it returns an **apparent** molar mass, and the van't Hoff factor $i$ must be put in:

$M_{2} = \dfrac{i\,K_{f}w_{2} \times 1000}{\Delta T_{f}w_{1}}$.

A measured molar mass half the true value is the classic sign of complete dissociation into two ions.

questions.q: $1.8$ g of glucose is dissolved in $250$ g of water. Find the boiling point of the solution. ($K_{b} = 0.52$ K kg/mol, molar mass of glucose $= 180$ g/mol.)
questions.solution:
**Moles of glucose:**

$n = \dfrac{1.8}{180} = 0.01$ mol.

**Molality:**

$m = \dfrac{0.01\text{ mol}}{0.250\text{ kg}} = 0.04$ mol/kg.

**Elevation:**

$\Delta T_{b} = K_{b}m = 0.52 \times 0.04 = 0.0208$ K.

**Boiling point:**

$T_{b} = 373.15 + 0.021 = \mathbf{373.17}$ K, or about $100.02$ °C.

Glucose is a non-electrolyte, so $i = 1$ and no correction is needed.

Notice how small the effect is: a hundredth of a degree for a gram and a half. That is why freezing-point depression ($K_{f}$ is more than three times larger, and easier to measure precisely) is preferred in the laboratory.

questions.q: What is the van't Hoff factor? Explain abnormal molar mass with one example of dissociation and one of association.
questions.solution:
**Definition.**

$i = \dfrac{\text{observed colligative property}}{\text{calculated (assuming no change)}} = \dfrac{\text{particles after}}{\text{particles before}}$.

Equivalently, $i = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{observed molar mass}}$.

**Dissociation ($i > 1$).** $\text{KCl}$ in water gives $\text{K}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$, so $i \approx 2$. The solution behaves as though it held twice as many particles, and the molar mass calculated from a colligative property comes out at about **half** the true value.

**Association ($i < 1$).** Acetic acid in benzene forms hydrogen-bonded **dimers**, so $i \approx 0.5$ and the apparent molar mass is about $120$ instead of $60$.

Neither is an error in the experiment. The experiment counts particles honestly; it is the assumption 'one molecule dissolved = one particle' that is wrong.

questions.q: State Henry's law and give two applications.
questions.solution:
**The law.** At constant temperature, the partial pressure of a gas above a solution is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution:

$p = K_{H}x$.

A **large** $K_{H}$ means a **low** solubility, and $K_{H}$ increases with temperature — gases dissolve less in warm liquids.

**Applications.**

1. **Fizzy drinks** are bottled under high $\text{CO}_{2}$ pressure. Opening the bottle drops the pressure, the solubility falls, and the gas comes out of solution.

2. **Deep-sea divers.** At depth, more nitrogen dissolves in the blood. Surfacing too fast releases it as bubbles in the bloodstream — decompression sickness, or 'the bends'. Diving cylinders therefore use helium in place of some of the nitrogen, since it is far less soluble.

3. **Climbers at high altitude** suffer anoxia because the low partial pressure of oxygen means less of it dissolves in the blood.

The same one line of algebra explains a soda bottle, a diver and a mountaineer.
